content_en: Trading gold on an XM KIWAMI account at 1 lot with 100,000 yen, a stop-out occurs after about $5.5 of adverse movement, so I had Gemini verify against IC and EBC. I thought IC would be the cheapest, but never expected EBC to win outright. EBC fixes leverage at 500x unless it's a special time such as before the weekend close. IC has HMR (margin rule), but it isn't as frequent as Exness, where leverage gets restricted before you notice. I'm concerned about EBC's recent blunder of being expelled from the Financial Commission. IC's weak points are deposits/withdrawals and support. [Corrected comparison table of effective drawdown tolerance and cost (100 oz / 15,000 yen = $1 conversion)] Accounts compared: (1) XM KIWAMI; (2) IC Markets (Raw/MT); (3) IC Markets (cTrader); (4) EBC Financial (PRO). Account funds: XM and IC are 100,000 yen at 1000x leverage; EBC is 500x leverage so 200,000 yen is assumed. Stop-loss (SL rate): XM 20% (9,000 yen remaining); both IC accounts 50% (22,500 yen remaining); EBC 30% (27,000 yen remaining). Initial trading cost (spread + commission): (1) about $1.50 (about 2,250 yen); (2) about $1.20 (about 1,800 yen); (3) about $1.10 (about 1,650 yen); (4) about $0.80 (about 1,200 yen). Effective tolerable loss (balance - cost - SL amount): (1) 88,750 yen; (2) 75,700 yen; (3) 75,850 yen; (4) 171,800 yen. Effective tolerable price range: (1) about $5.91 (measured $5.5-5.6); (2) about $5.04; (3) about $5.05; (4) about $11.45. Total round-trip cost per lot: (1) about $15.00 (2,250 yen); (2) about $12.00 (1,800 yen); (3) about $11.00 (1,650 yen); (4) about $8.00 (1,200 yen). Comparison of tolerance per account (with XM as the baseline): XM (100k / 1,000x / SL 20%) - effective tolerance about $5.5 to 5.9. Because you start in the minus by the spread the moment you enter, it falls short of the theoretical value ($6.07) and is stopped out near $5.5. IC Markets (100k / 1,000x / SL 50%) - effective tolerance about $4.7 to 5.0. Because the stop-out level is a high 50% (a balance of 22,500 yen is required), after deducting spread and commission it goes 0.8-0.9 dollars earlier than XM (below $5 to right around $5). It doesn't hold even $5.5, let alone $6. EBC Financial (200k / 500x / SL 30%) - effective tolerance about $11.0 to 11.4. Leverage drops to 500x (required margin 90,000 yen), but the advantage of raising funds to 200,000 yen is very large. The extremely narrow spread/commission cost (about $0.80) also contributes, and it can withstand about twice XM (the $11 range). Difference in total cost (per entry): EBC Pro about $8.00 (almost half of XM); IC cTrader about $11.00; IC Raw (MT4/5) about $12.00; XM KIWAMI about $15.00. For high-leverage, short-range scalping or tight fund management, the picture is 'XM, which can hold on to the limit with SL 20%' versus 'EBC, which withstands $11 with 200,000 yen funds while keeping trading costs lowest'.

Seeing the much-talked-about 'FX Warrior Kurumi-chan', there may be many girls who try 'I'll aim for 20 million yen from 300,000 yen too!' and ruin themselves. I support them 🔥 But there were no prop firms in Kurumi-chan's era; if you're taking revenge for your mother now, prop is more advantageous and easier. Many people still find prop troublesome and don't understand it well, so let me explain the difference between FX and prop a bit more simply. For example: if you put 300,000 yen of cash saved from a part-time job into an account at overseas high-leverage Exness, the rules are free, leverage is unlimited, you can do anything, and all profits can be withdrawn, but you can only use 300,000 yen. Another example: if you buy a 20-million-yen demo account (instant, going straight to a live phase) at prop firm FundedElite for 300,000 yen, you're bound by detailed rules such as leverage, but you can trade a 20-million-yen account until you lose 600,000 yen in a day or 1.2 million yen in total, and if you follow the rules properly you can withdraw the profits. That's roughly how it is. Account sizes go up to 35 million yen. If you have little money and keep melting small accounts with leverage, you should consider prop. If you're going all-in with all the savings you built up from part-time work, look into prop! In this world, using leverage like Kurumi-chan to turn 300,000 yen into 20 million isn't impossible, but well, the difficulty is high. #FXWarriorKurumi

I haven't experienced any inquiries from banks over withdrawals from Exness or XS. But I have experienced bank inquiries and account freezes several times. (1) Fintokei: a few phone confirmations from the bank. I think funds arrived from abroad around Czechia, and I got several calls asking 'This isn't money used for war or the like, is it?' (2) PayPay Bank: instant freeze with no questions asked. It's unclear whether overseas FX withdrawals were the cause; there was no inquiry from the bank and the account was frozen. I was still able to withdraw, though. (3) Mizuho Bank / SBI Bank: account frozen and withdrawals impossible. I got caught up in a P2P scam and the account was frozen; I couldn't even withdraw. This has nothing to do with overseas FX. Those are all the bank troubles I've experienced. In other words, even though I still repeat such large bank withdrawals, the only case where overseas FX withdrawals possibly affected my bank account is the single PayPay Bank freeze. And that was before the June 2026 revision of the Payment Services Act. At least in my experience, there hasn't been a single trouble confirmed as affected by the law revision. That doesn't mean it will necessarily be fine from now on, so I take measures such as splitting large withdrawals and leaving as little money as possible in the receiving bank account.

BLAZE Ver4.0 by dagram MASTER CLASS: after installing, when 'LONG' or 'STRONG BUY' appears near the upper limit of the band channel shown on the chart, and 'SELL' or 'STRONG SELL' near the lower limit, just enter as indicated. Recommended: gold, 3-minute and 5-minute charts. *It generally works on any symbol and any timeframe. dagram Fusion Oscillator *recommended together with BLAZE. *After applying -> once usage rights are granted, restart TradingView -> Indicators -> Invite-only and select it. It's an oscillator that integrates CCI, Williams %R, ADX and ATR into one to judge momentum, trend strength and volatility comprehensively. Role of each indicator: CCI: price momentum, overbought/oversold; Williams %R: timing of short-term reversals; ADX: trend strength; ATR: size of price movement. How to read signals: BUY: crossing above the 0 line + color turns green + BUY shown -> buyers dominant. SELL: crossing below the 0 line + color turns red + SELL shown -> sellers dominant. Strong trend: +40 or above: strong rise (buying dips favored); -40 or below: strong fall (selling rallies favored). *Oscillation around 0 (+/-10) or repeated BUY/SELL is likely a range, so skipping is recommended. How to use on the gold 3-minute chart: Long: Fusion crosses above the 0 line, new high, above the 20 EMA, Fusion at +20 or above. Short: Fusion crosses below the 0 line, new low, below the 20 EMA, Fusion at -20 or below. Points for raising the win rate: rather than a signal alone, combining the following reduces false signals: ADX > 25, ATR above a certain level, same direction as EMA50 and EMA200, high/low breakout, increased volume. Warning: this does not guarantee profit. It is an indicator developed to be used as a discretionary aid. #FX #Gold #Trade

Triggered by the post 'I was refused a 5-million-yen withdrawal at HFM', anxiety about overseas FX is spreading. Hearing that 5 million yen can't be withdrawn, it's only natural to be scared. But before checking the detailed circumstances and the broker's explanation, it's too early to assert HFM's financial condition or the cause this time. That said, if you use overseas FX, I think you should also consider 'risks other than losing in the market'. Even if trading is profitable, trouble can arise over withdrawals or the interpretation of the terms. In particular, with overseas brokers unregistered in Japan you can't assume the same user protection as with domestic ones, and pursuing problems is also difficult. This needs to be understood together with the high leverage and convenient features. So if you have sufficient funds, mainly trade discretionarily, and aren't struggling with the domestic trading environment, I would prioritize a domestic broker. The larger the amount you deposit, the more I'd value fund safeguarding and trouble-handling mechanisms. But EA users have different circumstances: - you need MT4 or MT5 that supports the EA you want to use; - you want to manage accounts and funds separately per EA; - you want to operate with less required margin. When you look for such conditions, overseas brokers remain candidates. Of course there are domestic brokers that support MT5 and EAs too, so you can't lump it together as 'unusable in Japan'. But once you include supported symbols, whether additional accounts are possible and trading conditions, whether it suits your use differs by broker. Overseas high leverage also lets you keep required margin low for the same trading volume, but if you increase lots just because you can hold more, losses grow accordingly. So I don't think 'overseas only, because funds are small' either; I'd compare including domestic minimum trading sizes. My view: if the needed conditions are available domestically, consider domestic first. If you need conditions that exist only overseas, confirm what risk you're taking on for that convenience. There's no need to carry only the custody risk when you're barely using overseas advantages. Conversely, I don't think everyone, including people with reasons to use overseas in terms of EAs or account management, has to make the same choice. What I'd like us to think about from this story is 'what am I depositing money with that broker for?' Whether you can explain that reason changes how you choose an account.

HFM has become a hot topic. I used it before too, but I stopped midway because I was bothered by the gap between the price I ordered and the price actually traded, and various other things felt off. Since this is a good opportunity, let me share a little of what I value when choosing a broker! First, narrow spreads are attractive, but that alone doesn't make a good broker. Especially for violently moving symbols like gold, you should check carefully: 1. how much the spread widens between normal times and economic data releases; 2. how much the price you ordered and the price actually traded differ; 3. whether a stop-loss turns out larger than planned; 4. how quickly a trade is filled after you press the order or close button. For example, suppose you tried to buy at 4,200 but actually bought at 4,202. That alone means you enter at a position $2 worse from the start. You might think 'is that all?', but as the number of trades grows it affects profit considerably. Of course price slippage itself happens at any broker, but what matters is how often and how much it deviates. The other important thing is withdrawals. Rather than putting in a large amount from the start, I recommend first trading with a small amount and checking that you can actually withdraw, including profits. Also check the number of days and conditions for withdrawal before depositing. No matter how good a trader you are, if the trading environment is bad, even the profit you should have been able to take shrinks. Especially for people who trade gold short-term, I think it's worth checking at least the execution deviation and withdrawal conditions.

The recent HFM account-ban and withdrawal-refusal matter is a hot topic, and I've written part of the story of when my own HFM account was banned last month in [table of contents 6-1] of this article. 'Articles 42 and 44 of the Client Agreement' can't be found anywhere on the site, and even when I asked I got no clear answer other than 'this is the final decision' - their handling is sloppy lol. Well, it's not only HFM that is sloppy; I think the large overseas FX brokers are all much the same... In my case, perhaps because the amount was relatively small, they still let me withdraw properly even after the ban, and since it's obvious that providing this EA's signals was the cause, I think it can't be helped. But seeing the 5-million-yen withdrawal refusal that's being talked about, I can't help suspecting that HFM may be in financial difficulty... Recently, too, it has started the KATANA account, which is like the GEMFOREX 'real zero account' and others rolled into one, to gather funds, and the USDJPY mission, also for gathering funds, ended early - it's getting suspicious. And now withdrawal refusal is in the news; if withdrawal delays start on top of this, it would be a complete GEMFOREX course... Well, at HFM you can't use bonuses across multiple accounts and they aren't handed out as recklessly as at GEMFOREX, so I can't tell whether the financial condition is bad. In any case, not just at HFM but in overseas FX generally, even if you're not paid out you basically have to just swallow it, so it really is better to withdraw often. I was thinking I'd withdraw in a lump sum later, and GEMFOREX went bankrupt without paying out, so I think that if you can speed up your withdrawal pace, you should do it before you regret it later.
With XM, bank withdrawals are fast for small amounts. It arrived about 10 minutes after the request, so I immediately deposited it into Titan FX.
